claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has moderate-to-high friction and wear, particularly at elevated temperatures.
Applying a thin, self-adaptive, functionally graded self-lubricating coating will reduce friction across room temperature to 800 °C.
The proposed coating will reduce wear across room temperature to 800 °C.
A thermally driven transition in lubrication mechanism will produce the broad-temperature friction and wear improvements.
A thin coating can be deposited as a film on a substrate.
The proposed coating is a single-layer, functionally graded, self-lubricating coating designed to form lubricious oxides.
At lower temperatures, the coating will maintain a dense, adherent barrier.
At higher temperatures, the coating will promote formation of a lubricious dopant-derived oxide at the sliding interface.
At room temperature, the coating's tuned microstructure will provide a low-shear interface.
Controlled oxidation at elevated temperature will create a lubricious oxide layer that minimizes direct asperity contact.
Minimizing direct asperity contact will maintain low friction and reduce wear.
The coated sample will have consistently lower coefficient of friction than bare CoCrFeNi at every tested temperature through 800 °C.
The coated sample will have consistently lower wear rate than bare CoCrFeNi at every tested temperature through 800 °C.
The coating's benefit will be especially significant at high temperatures.
The hypothesis is limited to ambient-air sliding from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C under typical load and speed regimes.
The coating's precise composition and intermediate-temperature phase evolution are uncertain.
The coating's long-term stability under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading is unverified.
A controlled comparison of bare and coated CoCrFeNi samples will measure friction, wear-track volume or depth, morphology, and oxide formation over the stated temperature range.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both friction and wear consistently across the entire temperature range will falsify the hypothesis.
